topics: 🍖 Ben Drosai's Measure — how much cooking makes food 'done enough' before Shabbat
🪵 Kindling a Bonfire Before Shabbat — how much of it must already have caught fire
🕯️ Four Bonfires That Never Need 'Most of It' to Catch
🎬 Chapter's End — 'Hadran' on Yetziot HaShabbat, and a new mishna begins
🧵 With What May One Kindle? — the new mishna's list of forbidden wicks and oils

overview.title: 📖 Overview: From Ben Drosai to a New Chapter
overview.subtitle: Shabbat 20a–20b
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf opens by quantifying the mishna's requirement that food be roasted 'while it is still day': Rav's standard is the partial roasting of the outlaw ben Drosai, who could never wait for food to fully cook. The Gemara then works out how much of a bonfire — or a single branch, or bundled reeds and seeds — must have caught fire before Shabbat, weighing Rav's and Shmuel's competing standards and testing them against four kinds of fuel (pitch, sulfur, cheese, fat) that ignite so easily no threshold is needed. This closes the first chapter, Yetziot HaShabbat, with the formal 'Hadran' marker. A new mishna and chapter, Bameh Madlikin, then opens with a detailed list of wicks and oils disqualified for the Shabbat lamp — the topic the Gemara will spend the next several dafim identifying and explaining.

slides.title: 🍖 How Much Roasting Counts as 'Done'?
slides.subtitle: The standard for letting food finish cooking after Shabbat begins

steps.content: 1️⃣ Rav (via Rabbi Elazar): sufficiently roasted means like the food of ben Drosai — a fugitive who never had time to fully cook his food, so 'partially roasted'
2️⃣ Rabbi Yochanan adds: once food reaches that stage by a Jew, a gentile finishing the cooking afterward creates no problem of 'gentile-cooked food'
3️⃣ Chananya: once food is cooked like ben Drosai's, it may be kept on a stove on Shabbat even if the stove is not swept of coals or covered with ash
4️⃣ Practical result: 'ben Drosai' becomes the recurring halakhic threshold for 'no longer a concern that someone will stoke the coals'

callout.label: Same word, resolved question:
callout.text: The Gemara also settles a dilemma about the mishna's phrase 'until the bottom crust forms': it means the surface stuck to the oven wall, not the side nearest the fire — proven from Rabbi Eliezer's own more explicit wording.

slides.title: 🪵 What Fraction of the Wood Must Have Caught Fire?
slides.subtitle: Rival standards for reeds, seeds, and single branches
rows: Rav Huna: reeds catch easily on their own
Once tied, they behave like a solid beam
Majority must catch (Rav Kahana reverses Rav Huna's cases)
Rav Chisda: scattered items actually burn worse, not better
Most of its thickness AND its circumference (Rav Pappa, combining both versions of Rav's ruling)
Ambiguity in how 'most' was transmitted led to the stricter combined standard

callout.label: Four exceptions:
callout.text: Rav Yosef taught that bonfires of pitch, sulfur, dry cheese, or fatty material never need a majority to catch — and a further baraita adds straw and field rakings, since all of these ignite instantly once touched by flame.

slides.title: 🔥 Rav vs. Shmuel: What Counts as 'Most of the Bonfire'?
slides.subtitle: Two very different tests for the same mishna phrase

lines.speaker: Rav
lines.text: 'Most of it' means most of the thickness of each individual branch in the pile must have caught fire.

lines.speaker: Shmuel
lines.text: It's enough that the fire has taken hold well enough that no one would say, 'Bring thinner branches and put them underneath to help it along.'

lines.speaker: Rav Chiyya
lines.text: Support for Shmuel, from the Temple candelabrum: it must be lit so the flame rises on its own, not because something else is propping it up.

lines.speaker: Gemara
lines.text: This mirrors a tannaitic dispute: Rabbi Chiyya says wood counts as 'burnt' once ruined for a craftsman's use; Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira requires fire on both sides — with a scriptural allusion from Ezekiel 15:4.

callout.label: The stakes:
callout.text: If not enough of the bonfire has caught before Shabbat, one might be tempted to stoke or rearrange the wood on Shabbat itself — a real melacha.

slides.title: 🎬 Hadran — The First Chapter Ends
slides.text: With the discussion of Babylonian cedar wood and hyssop needing no majority to catch fire, the Gemara reaches הדרן עלך יציאות השבת — 'we shall return to you, Yetziot HaShabbat' — the formal close of tractate Shabbat's first chapter, which opened with the laws of carrying objects between domains on Shabbat eve. A new mishna immediately opens the second chapter, Bameh Madlikin ('With what may one kindle'), turning from carrying to the laws of the Shabbat lamp.

slides.title: 🧵 The New Mishna's Two Lists: Forbidden Wicks and Forbidden Oils
slides.subtitle: Materials that may not be used to light the Shabbat lamp

boxes.title: Forbidden Wicks
items: Lekhesh — the woolly substance under cedar bark
Chosen — flax stalk that was crushed but not yet combed
Kalach — the cocoon of a silkworm (Rav Yitzchak bar Ze'ira)
Petilat ha'idan (willow) and petilat hamidbar (mullein) — both burn poorly
Green moss floating on the surface of standing water

boxes.title: Forbidden Oils
items: Shemen kik — oil from the castor-like plant of Jonah
Shemen sereifa — 'burnt oil,' impure teruma oil
Elya (tail fat) and chelev (forbidden animal fat)
Nachum HaMadi permits boiled chelev; the Sages disagree entirely

callout.label: Why they fail:
callout.text: Wool and hair were added by a later baraita, though the mishna's own tanna didn't bother — wool shrinks and hair scorches when burned, so no one would think to try them as wicks anyway.

summary.principle: The mishna's requirement that cooking or kindling be well underway before Shabbat is quantified concretely — 'ben Drosai' for food, 'most of the wood' for a bonfire — and the chapter closes by pivoting from carrying to the new subject of what may and may not fuel the Shabbat lamp.

flowSteps.content: 🍖 Ben Drosai's partial roast sets the threshold for food left to finish cooking through Shabbat
🪵 How much of a bonfire, branch, or bundle must catch fire before dark? Rav and Shmuel disagree on the test

columns.content: 🕯️ Pitch, sulfur, cheese, fat: always exempt from the majority rule

flowSteps.content: 🧵 New mishna opens chapter 2: a detailed catalogue of forbidden wicks and forbidden oils for the Shabbat lamp
🎓 Key Principle: whatever burns unreliably, smells bad, or requires tending is unfit — both for cooking left to finish and for the Shabbat lamp itself

quiz.q: What is the halakhic standard, attributed to ben Drosai, for how much food must be roasted before Shabbat for it to be permitted to finish cooking?
o: Fully cooked and ready to eat
Partially roasted, like the hurried cooking of a fugitive who could not wait
Merely placed on the fire, with no cooking required yet
Cooked for exactly one hour
quiz.e: Rav (via Rabbi Elazar) teaches that the standard is 'like the food of ben Drosai' — partially roasted, since ben Drosai was a fugitive who could never wait for food to fully cook.

quiz.q: According to Shmuel, what determines whether 'most of' a bonfire has caught fire before Shabbat?
o: Most of the thickness of each individual branch must be burning
It's enough that no one would say 'bring thinner wood to help it along'
The entire pile must be reduced to ash
Only the outermost branches need to catch
quiz.e: Shmuel's standard is functional: the fire must have taken hold well enough that observers wouldn't feel the need to add thinner kindling to help it burn — supported by the parallel rule for the Temple candelabrum.

quiz.q: According to the baraita, which four types of material never require that 'most of it' catch fire before Shabbat?
o: Wood, straw, wool, and hair
Pitch, sulfur, dry cheese, and fatty material
Reeds, date seeds, flax, and cedar
Olive oil, wax, tar, and naphtha
quiz.e: Rav Yosef taught that bonfires of pitch (zefet), sulfur (gofrit), dry cheese, and fatty material (revav) ignite so readily that no threshold of 'most of it' is required.

quiz.q: What does the 'Hadran' formula on this daf mark?
o: The conclusion of the entire tractate Shabbat
The end of the first chapter, Yetziot HaShabbat, before a new chapter and mishna begin
A break for a different tractate entirely
The start of the laws of Chanukah
quiz.e: 'הדרן עלך יציאות השבת' marks the formal close of chapter one, Yetziot HaShabbat; the Gemara immediately continues with the new mishna 'Bameh Madlikin,' opening chapter two.

quiz.q: According to the Gemara's identification of terms in the new mishna, what is 'kalach,' one of the forbidden wicks?
o: A type of olive oil
The cocoon of a silkworm
Ordinary sheep's wool
Willow bark
quiz.e: Rav Yitzchak bar Ze'ira identifies kalach as gushkera, the cocoon of the silkworm — while Shmuel says seafarers called it by the name kulka.
